transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Welcome to the American Express Q2 2026 Earnings Call. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. I will now turn the call over to Kartik Ramachandran, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Kartik Ramachandran
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Thank you, and thank you all for joining today's call. Today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about the company's future business and financial performance. These are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements are included in today's presentation slides and in our reports on file with the SEC. Today's discussion also contains non-GAAP financial measures. Comparable GAAP financial measures are included in this quarter's earnings materials as well as the prior period earnings materials discussed today. All of these are posted on our website at ir.americanexpress.com. We will begin today with Steve Squeri, Chairman and CEO; followed by Christophe Le Caillec, Chief Financial Officer. After their remarks, we'll move to Q&A. With that, I'll turn it over to Steve.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thank you, Kartik. Good morning, and thanks for joining us today. We delivered another excellent quarter with 10% revenue growth and EPS of $4.53. Our results continue the momentum we've seen over the last few quarters and reinforce the confidence that we have in our strategy for sustaining long-term growth. Based on our better-than-expected performance year-to-date, we are raising our full year revenue growth guidance to 10%, and we plan to reinvest this outperformance in growth initiatives across our business. We continue to expect full year EPS of $17.30 to $17.90. I'm sure the question on your minds right now is if you're outperforming your expectations, and you are raising your revenue guidance, why aren't you also raising EPS guidance? I'll answer it. We have a choice. We can either drop the overperformance to the bottom line and buy back more shares or we can invest to grow the business further through the wide range of attractive growth opportunities we have across our business, both in the U.S. and international. We've chosen the latter. Because in the long run, it is the one that creates the most value for our shareholders as demonstrated by our high ROE. That is what we have consistently done over the past several years. As we're at the halfway point of the year, let me take a step back and walk you through how we approach this year and how our results reflect the strength of our business model and the strategic decisions we've made to position the company for long-term success. Over a year ago, consistent with our strategic focus on strengthening our leadership in the premium space, we made the decision to make a significant investment in enhancing our flagship Platinum products in the U.S. While I've said this before, it's worth repeating. When we invest in a product refresh, we expect to realize the full benefits of a year or two after launch. First, we anticipate increased customer engagement as well as strong demand and spend growth. Then as we lap the investments and as the new fees kick in over time, we expect fee revenues to increase and VCE expense growth to moderate. And by focusing on bringing in high credit quality premium customers, we expect to see consistently strong credit performance, which supports strong earnings growth. With that in mind, as we enter 2026, our plan was as follows: make the upfront investments in the Platinum value propositions, which we anticipated would continue to drive the high pace of revenue growth; maintain strong credit risk management; and drive operating leverage across our marketing and operating expenses. The combination of high revenue growth, strong credit performance and disciplined expense management were key elements of our plan for driving mid-teens EPS growth for the fourth consecutive year. Six months into the year, we're seeing stronger momentum than we expected. The investments we made in our value propositions have driven accelerated spend and revenue growth, and our Platinum portfolio is now the fastest growing in our U.S. consumer business. Our credit performance is also better than we expected. Retention rates remain very high, and we continue to attract a large number of highly creditworthy customers with 65% of new consumer accounts coming from Millennials and Gen Z. Importantly, we've continued to deliver strong revenue and earnings growth while at the same time being able to invest more in customer acquisition and technology. Over the course of the year we will continue to capitalize on the growth opportunities that position the company for long-term success. In looking to the second half of the year, we have great momentum. We expect card fee growth to accelerate, credit to continue to be very strong and variable card member engagement growth to decelerate as we lap the Platinum refresh of last year. As the Platinum refresh laps, the key to our growth momentum over the past several years has been our focus on investing in and innovating our membership-based value propositions to attract and engage premium customers across generations and geographies. Creating compelling premium value propositions that are competitively differentiated is not just about reward points. It's about enabling spending power, providing access to highly desirable travel, dining, entertainment and exclusive experiences, forging relationships with world-class partners who provide additional value, and having talented, dedicated colleagues who back our customers and merchant partners when issues arise. In essence, a great premium value proposition is not just a product. It's a multifaceted relationship between the brand and the customer. This is what our membership model delivers, and it is very difficult to replicate on a global scale. To build deep, enduring relationships with our premium customers, we've leaned into adding benefits they value and where they spend like travel, which is why we continue to expand our lounge and luxury hotel networks. And dining, which is why we acquired Resy and Tock and the proposed acquisition of TheFork, a leading online restaurant booking platform, which Resy would add 50,000 restaurants to our dining network across 11 European countries. It's also why we've added new sports sponsorships like the NFL and Fanatics and provide access to a wide variety of exclusive membership experiences around the world. Deepening the engagement with our premium customers is also why we continue to introduce new digital payment capabilities such as the recent announcement that card members can redeem Membership Rewards points directly within Apple Pay, giving them greater flexibility to use their points on everyday purchases. A core element in designing our value propositions is working with world-class partners who value the opportunity to reach our high-spending premium card members. We're expanding partnerships with many of the premier companies in the world across a range of industries that further enrich the value of membership and drive customer engagement. In fact, just a few days ago, we announced a new global partnership with ALL - Accor Live Limitless, the booking and loyalty platform for Accor's portfolio of 45 worldwide hotel brands, which include Raffles, Fairmont and Sofitel. Importantly, our approach to creating value propositions is not a one-size-fits-all exercise. It is tailored to meet the needs and preferences of different customers and in different locations. For example, the Platinum Card is designed for customers who value premium travel and lifestyle perks like airport lounge access, luxury hotel benefits and one-of-a-kind experiences. The Gold Card, on the other hand, is designed for those who do some traveling but prioritize their spending on dining, grocery and other everyday benefits. Likewise, our co-brand cards each have their own value propositions with benefits that appeal to their specific customer bases. And our value propositions for small- and medium-sized business customers are designed to fit the different payment and financial management needs of their businesses. For example, in the second quarter, we introduced the $300 ChatGPT business annual statement credit for our U.S. Business Platinum and Gold Card members, and we launched a pilot of our new expense management platform to an initial group of middle market customers. We've been executing the same strategy internationally, creating premium value propositions with benefits, partnerships and experiences that are tailored to customer needs and local dynamics in each geography at price points that are typically higher than in the U.S. Since 2003, we've refreshed our Platinum Card in approximately 80% of the countries where these cards are issued, which has helped to drive 20% FX-adjusted growth in international Platinum card spending this year. Furthermore, around 70% of new consumer Platinum Card accounts outside the U.S. are coming from Millennials and Gen Z. This approach to innovating our premium value propositions has served us well, and we plan to continue implementing this successful playbook across our business. As a result, we have built a business that compounds earnings more durably and at a faster pace than in the past. When compared to our historical performance, we now have more momentum in both the top and bottom lines, a more premium fee-paying customer base with strong loyalty, less credit risk, including less risk under stress, and more younger customers who represent greater lifetime value. In sum, we are competing from a position of strength. We are tracking ahead of the expectations we set at the beginning of the year, generating momentum that enables us to invest more in 2026 than we initially planned and in opportunities that drive long-term growth. In fact, our proposed acquisition of TheFork is one of those great opportunities. We did not have it originally in our plan at the beginning of the year and it will require investment in the second half of the year. As our strong performance has shown, we are winning with the next generation of premium customers and we have significant growth opportunities across our businesses and around the world. Taken together, this gives us confidence in our long runway for sustainable growth and our ability to continue delivering attractive returns for our shareholders. I'll now turn it over to Christophe for details on the quarter.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Thanks, Steve, and good morning, everyone. We had another strong quarter with revenue growth of 10% and EPS up 11% year-over-year. Pretax income was up 15%, while net income was up 8% due to prior year tax discretes. The strength of our premium customer base combined with the success of our product strategy has driven accelerated momentum in the first half of the year. Spend growth stepped up to the highest level we've seen in three years, up 9% FX-adjusted, in both Q1 and Q2, and balanced growth continued to keep pace with spending. Demand for our premium products remains strong with over 70% of new accounts acquired on fee-based products this year. And card fees have now grown at a double-digit rate for 32 consecutive quarters. Importantly, our focus on premium products continues to drive improvements in credit performance. The strengthening we have seen in our credit performance is a deliberate outcome of our strategy to invest in value propositions that attract customers with high credit quality. As a result of that strategy, both delinquency and write-off rates remain below 2019 levels and delinquency rates have been between 1.2% and 1.3% for over three years. The combination of top line momentum, excellent credit and disciplined expense management have together supported 11% revenue growth and 14% EPS growth through the first half of the year even as we have invested in our U.S. Platinum value propositions. These results demonstrate the strength of our model and give us confidence in our ability to drive sustainable growth in line with our long-term aspiration. Turning to Billed Business trends for the quarter: Overall spend was up 9.4% FX-adjusted, almost 1 point higher than Q1. Growth was broad-based across categories with goods and services spending up 9% and T&E up 10%. Retail spending continued to be very strong, up 13% FX-adjusted in the quarter. Restaurant spending, our largest T&E category, was up 10%. And line spending picked up further from the strong growth we saw in Q1, also up 10% year-over-year. Our customers are showing strong demand for travel with global MX travel bookings up 22% year-over-year in the quarter. U.S. consumer spending was up 11%, the highest level of growth since Q1 2018, excluding periods impacted by the pandemic. And we continue to see good engagement from our younger customers. Millennials and Gen Z, which make up the larger share of U.S. consumer spending, remained our fastest-growing cohorts this quarter. Commercial spending picked up to 5% with both U.S. SME and large global customers growing at the same pace. We are still in the early stages of our commercial product roadmap but we are encouraged by recent trends. At the same time, we do expect to see impacts from the sale of the small business co-brand portfolios in the balance of the year, which I will get to a bit later when I discuss our outlook. International also delivered another strong quarter. Spend was up 12% FX-adjusted. Growth remains broad-based across consumer and business customers and across geographies with four of our top five countries growing at a double-digit rate. Turning to new card acquisitions: We acquired three million new cards in the quarter with continued momentum in acquiring younger customers and attracting new customers onto our fee-paying products. Looking at balance growth and credit: Total balances increased 9% year-over-year FX-adjusted, in line with Billed Business. We have now lapped the roughly 1 percentage point impact on balance growth from when the small business co-brand portfolios were classified as held for sale over a year ago. As a reminder, although these two portfolios were classified as held for sale, we continued to earn economics until the transfer of the portfolios to the new issuers. One portfolio transfer happened in April this year and the second one is expected in Q3. Credit performance continues to be very strong. The Q2 write-off rate was flat versus last quarter while the delinquency rate declined. Provision expense of $1.1 billion included a reserve release of $191 million, mostly reflecting further strengthening of portfolio credit performance. The strength of our model also holds in a stressed environment as demonstrated by the Fed's recently released CCAR results, which show that under a severely adverse scenario, we have the lowest projected credit card loss rate across all banks and a pretax ROE of 3.8% over nine quarters. Turning to revenue: Revenue was up 10%, marking our fourth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Net card fees reached record levels, and once again were our fastest-growing line, up 15.4%. We continue to see good momentum in attracting customers onto our premium products with 75% of new accounts acquired on fee-paying products in the quarter, the highest level we have seen since we increased our focus on premium products. Net interest income was up 11% this quarter. We saw around a 1 percentage point impact to year-over-year NII growth from the sale of one of the small business co-brand portfolios. We continue to grow balances largely in line with spending while driving higher NII growth by expanding the margin earned on balances. We are also seeing demand for our deposit products with balances from our U.S. consumer and small business banking deposit products up 9% year-over-year. The majority of deposits come from our card members, deepening their engagement with our membership model. And with around 10% of our U.S. card members currently holding a deposit account with us, we see a long runway for growth. Turning to expenses: Marketing and OpEx each grew 6% in the quarter. And the VCE to revenue ratio was 44.6%. The step-up versus the first half of last year reflects the investment we made in the value propositions of our U.S. Platinum cards when we refreshed these products in September last year. As we discussed at the start of the year, the VCE to revenue ratio is linked to the level of card member spending. Through the first half of the year, we have seen stronger spend than we expected coming into the year, including in categories like airlines, where customers earn and use rewards. These factors are contributing to a slightly higher VCE ratio than we originally expected. Moving on to capital: We returned $2.9 billion of capital to our shareholders, including $0.6 billion of dividends and $2.2 billion of share repurchases. Our business continues to generate very strong returns with an ROE of 36% this quarter. Our strong ROE enables us to return high levels of earnings to our shareholders — over 75% over the past three years. Turning to our 2026 outlook. Let me spend a few minutes on how we're thinking about the balance of year. Starting with billings and revenue: We expect to see impacts from the sale of the two small business co-brand portfolios. The transfers of the portfolios are staggered across Q2 and Q3, building to the full impact by Q4. Starting in Q4, we expect a quarterly impact of around 1 percentage point to spend growth and around a 2.5 percentage point impact to net interest income until we lap the portfolio sales. Put together, the impact to total revenue is about 1 percentage point. I would note that the portfolio sales will have a negligible impact to pretax income, and these impacts were incorporated in the guidance we provided for the year. On card fees, we expect growth to accelerate in Q3 and to exit the year in the high teens, and we continue to expect credit metrics to be generally stable throughout the year. Turning to expenses: We expect marketing to be up by around 10% year-over-year in the second half of the year, driven by increased investments in customer acquisition. We continue to expect operating expenses to grow in the mid-single digits for the full year, including the additional investment in technology we previously discussed. On the VCE ratio, given the higher level of spending we have seen this year, we now expect the ratio to be between 44% and 45% for the full year. We will lap the impacts of the Platinum refresh starting in Q4, resulting in lower growth in VCE expenses. We feel really good about our momentum and our results halfway through the year, having delivered 11% revenue growth and 14% EPS growth as well as the opportunities for continued growth ahead. Given the momentum in the business, we are raising our revenue guidance and now expect full year revenue growth of 10%. And as we increase investments in new customer acquisition and technology development, we are maintaining our full year EPS guidance of $17.30 to $17.90. The guidance does not include the potential impact from the sale of our equity interest in Global Business Travel Group that we previously announced. We expect the transaction to close in the second half of the year and will provide more detail then. With that, I'll turn the call back over to Kartik, and we'll take your questions.

transcript.speaker: Kartik Ramachandran
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Thank you, Christophe. We will now start the Q&A session. We ask that you please limit yourself to just one question. Thank you for your cooperation. Operator?

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Our first question today is coming from Sanjay Sakhrani of KBW.

transcript.speaker: Sanjay Sakhrani
transcript.title: Analyst - KBW
transcript.content: So the 11-plus percent growth in U.S. Consumer Services is truly impressive. I'm curious if there's a way to parse apart how much is coming as a result of the strong account acquisitions you've seen of late versus your core mature customers spending more on the card. I'm just trying to think about the sustainability of that outperformance. And then also, it's really impressive this is happening amid geopolitical impacts and obviously the contagion to the economy. I'm just curious if you're seeing anything on that front, whether it's in U.S. Consumer Services or in other areas.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Sanjay. So on U.S. consumer billing, you're absolutely correct — it's up 11.4%. We went back in time to see when was the last time we saw such growth, and if you strip out the discontinuity of COVID, you have to go back to Q1 2018. So it's truly an impressive performance. One of the biggest contributors to the acceleration is the Platinum refresh. It is, by far, the biggest product we have and it has the fastest growth rate. There's truly a lot of momentum. We see that momentum coming from new card member acquisition as well as tenured card members that are increasing their spend, as well as people who have another card in their wallet and are upgrading to the Platinum card. Platinum is definitely pulling a lot here in the acceleration. If you go back to Q1, we quantified that acceleration, and I talked about it in the Q1 numbers: we noted a 600 basis point acceleration across the entire Platinum portfolio in U.S. consumer. So it's truly coming from a lot of tenured card members that are consolidating their spend because they enjoy the new value proposition.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yes, Sanjay, let me just add a couple of points. I think with the refresh, engagement has been really accelerated, and that's driving a lot of the spend. When you start to dig into the numbers, we saw a 22% increase in travel bookings. We put that into the value proposition. You look at restaurant spend, which was up 10%, but when you look at Resy restaurant spend, it's double that. So again, I think what we've hit on really well here with the Platinum refresh is we're stepping up engagement. So I think as Christophe said, it's a combination of new acquisition and the engagement that we're getting with existing card members, and it is very impressive to be at 11% at this stage of the game.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: And to the second part of your question about the geopolitical events out there: when you look at granular data, you do see gas spend increasing significantly. Now it's around 2% of total billings, so it's not meaningful in terms of impact to the overall numbers. You do see travel routing through the Middle East having some impact, as you would expect. But travel globally is up 10%, and this is the highest number — airline is up 10% — we've seen in the last six quarters. So there are some impacts, but there is no evidence of a general slowdown. People are offsetting these transactions with transactions in other categories, so it's not really visible at a macro level.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Ryan Nash of Goldman Sachs.

transcript.speaker: Ryan Nash
transcript.title: Analyst - Goldman Sachs
transcript.content: So Steve, you noted the decision to reinvest the upside in revenue growth. Maybe just talk a little bit more about the areas that you're investing in. I know you referenced customer acquisition and technology and maybe just talk a little bit about what you think this will do in terms of your ability to sustain these types of top line growth levels into 2027?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Okay. Thanks for the question. Look, I think we've gotten to a point where the company has got quite large and to continue the revenue growth, it requires us to continue to invest. Those investments come across a wide range. The one thing I did call out was we're pursuing the acquisition of TheFork; if all things work out, that will require deal costs and integration costs. We're investing in technology. When you think about our company, we've got international business, U.S. business, corporate card business, small business; we operate in many different countries. We have a merchant acquiring business and a network business. There is no shortage of technology investments or enhancements or refreshes that need to occur. Across a wide range of technology platforms, we're able to pull some of those investments into the second half of the year. To be able to get to things quicker is a huge advantage because we've got a large backlog of technology projects and getting to them sooner allows us to update platforms and deliver capabilities faster. The other area is card acquisition opportunities. To sustain growth, you need to continue to invest in acquiring high revenue-generating and high-spending cardholders. That's where you can think about these investments occurring: in technology, TheFork, and in card acquisition. You've also seen we've announced a number of things we're participating in from an agentic commerce perspective, and that requires investment as well. Those things weren't on the docket at the beginning of the year. It's not a stagnant business, and it's not a business where you don't need to put gas in the tank. That's what we're doing. It's a strategy we've employed for a number of years and it's served us well — we've been consistently growing over the last four years with double-digit revenue growth and mid-teens EPS growth. We look at the medium to long term and we think this is the best strategy for us and our shareholders.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Don Fandetti of Wells Fargo.

transcript.speaker: Donald Fandetti
transcript.title: Analyst - Wells Fargo
transcript.content: Steve, it sounds like you're feeling a little bit better about SME, and you launched a pilot on the expense management software. I guess I'm trying to understand: is this more of a discussion around the pace of billed business growth? Or could we see some type of middle market customers moving away to the fintechs where there could be some lumpiness? And then my follow-up is just to touch on the advantage of the closed loop around agentic commerce.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Okay. Thanks for the question, Don. We announced an aggressive commercial card roadmap earlier in the year. You're seeing a bit of a bounce back: SME billed business was up 5% and large global customers were up 5% as well. From a middle market space, we've seen some softness historically, but small business has been very strong and large/global corporate has been moving along nicely. Center, our expense management system which we just launched in pilot, should help us retain and win new business in middle market. We've seen an uptick in SME billings over the last two quarters, and the product roadmap and the launch of the middle market expense management software will certainly help us. On agentic commerce, the closed loop has been discussed for many years — in the physical world and in e-commerce. We're even more advantaged from an e-commerce perspective because of fraud, data, and the ability to understand intent. When you think about agentic commerce and how broad it is, beyond fraud there's also the risk of hallucinations in AI. By understanding what a card member truly wants — their intent — and having that data, and by matching that with purchase data, we can provide and back our customers much better. That's why we announced the agentic insurance product months ago, where we think we'll have a huge advantage from a trust, service and security perspective over competitors because we have data on both sides: we know what the customer wanted to do and we can know what the merchant delivered. People are in the very early innings here — we're in pre-season, not even early innings of the regular season. People are a little nervous interacting in this space, but we hope because of our knowledge of both sides of the equation, as agentic commerce takes off, customers and partners will choose us because of our ability and our historical track record of backing our customers. We've seen the closed loop advantage in the physical world and in e-commerce; we believe it's going to play out even more over time.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Craig Maurer of FT Partners.

transcript.speaker: Craig Maurer
transcript.title: Analyst - FT Partners
transcript.content: Wanted to ask about the adjustment in the URR and how material the benefit was in the quarter? That helps us gauge the rest of the year and when you lap it next year. Additionally, you talked about higher client incentives and business development expense. Can you talk about those trends considering the big wins you've had recently with the NFL, Fanatics and so on?

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: I'll take the URR question. The URR, for those who are not familiar, is part of the key element of our Membership Rewards program; we evaluate and quantify the ultimate rate of redemption. From an accounting standpoint, we expense the cost of those rewards when they are earned and we make an assumption about how many of those points ultimately are going to be redeemed. It's a fairly complex calculation, and on a regular basis we update the models and improve the data that feeds the model to be more accurate. As you can imagine, there's a lot of review and work that goes into any revision of that assumption. When we did our update, we came up with a slightly lower ultimate rate of redemption, but it really hasn't changed it much. We report externally that the ultimate rate of redemption is around 96%, and it really hasn't changed materially. So it had a small benefit in the quarter in terms of Membership Rewards cost, but at the full year level it's de minimis. It's more hygiene and making sure we have the right accounting process than anything else.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thanks for the question, Craig. When we think about the NFL, Fanatics, and our other sponsorships like the NBA, Formula 1, the USGA, Wimbledon and U.S. Open tennis, sponsorships are all about access for our card members and the experiences we can create. That's why we have event and stadium benefits in various locations around the world. We're packaging up groups of experiences our card members really like, including music and artist access. Specifically with the NFL and Fanatics, it gives us global access for our card members to events and venues they want to attend. Fanatics ties it together not only from an experience perspective with Fanatics Fest and presence at the NFL Draft, All-Star Games, Super Bowl, etc., but also from a collectibles and trading card perspective. From a cost perspective, when you think about our entire marketing budget, it's very small; these sponsorships are in the plan and in the run rate. So when we talk about increased investments, those sponsorships are not the primary incremental items we're adding. We like the assets we have, how they work together, and how our card members enjoy them.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Rick Shane of JPMorgan.

transcript.speaker: Richard Shane
transcript.title: Analyst - JPMorgan
transcript.content: You guys have talked a lot about customer acquisition. Can we talk a little bit about attrition, both quantitatively and qualitatively? Can we sort of think through what the one- to two-year retention rates are on new customers versus what you've seen historically? And also, to the extent you get feedback when customers don't renew the card, what are the reasons that a customer might walk away?

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: The executive summary is: we're not seeing any meaningful change in attrition. We showed a detailed slide in Q1 on the Platinum card where we raised the fee by $200. By the end of Q1 we had repriced about a quarter of the U.S. Platinum portfolio, and the retention rates were through the roof and flat year-over-year. There was no meaningful price-induced attrition. In terms of why people downgrade or leave, sometimes customers say they've retired and they don't need the benefits anymore and choose to downgrade. Conversely, we've seen many card members upgrading as a result of the new value proposition. In general, attrition levels remain very consistent with what we've seen in the past; they remain very low. We've been refreshing many of our products and repricing new card members, and the end result is that attrition levels have stayed very constant and very low for the past few years.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Mark DeVries of Deutsche Bank.

transcript.speaker: Mark DeVries
transcript.title: Analyst - Deutsche Bank
transcript.content: Steve, how should we think about the longer-term return on investment in platforms like Resy and TheFork? There are benefits like the lift to spend in the category, but also less obvious benefits such as revenues from the platforms and higher loyalty with merchants and customers. Any longer-term plans to integrate those platforms and maybe rebrand?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thanks for the questions, Mark. With Resy, Tock and TheFork, what we've tried to do is create many closed loops within our closed loop. We're connecting our card members and merchants, and these platforms are open, so they're also useful for non-card members from an acquisition perspective. Within those platforms we'll provide special offers and table access for card members — an opportunity to acquire card members more cheaply and for non-card members to experience the benefits of being a card member. We don't look at Resy, Tock, or TheFork as stand-alone P&Ls; we view them as part of the value proposition. Restaurants see that as access to our best customers who will spend more at their establishment. The proof is the outcomes: spend at Resy restaurants is two times higher for our card members and ticket prices are higher for card members versus non-card members. Resy and Tock will come together from a front-end user experience perspective to provide a more integrated restaurant experience, and TheFork, given its European focus, will remain a standalone entity for now and that works. Our travel representatives will have access to all these platforms, so when you book travel, they can also book restaurants for you. We don't manage Resy, Tock, and TheFork on a P&L basis; we manage them as benefits that drive card member retention, customer acquisition, merchant satisfaction and spend. They integrate well with our travel business and add capability for our travel representatives.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: I'll add a finance overlay. There's a lot more momentum now than 10–15 years ago: faster product refresh cycles, faster revenue momentum and billing growth. The balance sheet and portfolio resilience are stronger now. For example, our reserve rate has come down from 2.9% at the end of 2019 to 2.7% now — an outcome of focusing on premium card members. Card fees have grown significantly; that line has grown at 17% over the last seven years because a lot more card members are paying fees. In stress testing, the Fed results show we have much lower peak write-off rates than peers and remain profitable through the cycle. Finally, focusing on younger card members gives us confidence in our ability to sustain growth — they come with lower initial income but we grow with them and they represent a lot of embedded future growth.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Terry Ma of Barclays.

transcript.speaker: Terry Ma
transcript.title: Analyst - Barclays
transcript.content: Can you give a little more color on your net card fee growth guidance in the back half of this year, what's contemplated in that — whether it's just from step-ups in the back book annual fees or are you contemplating more acquisitions? Historically you've seen a notable acceleration after a refresh and you haven't seen that thus far at Platinum; any color?

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Terry, let me explain. We're growing card fees at 15% year-to-date. We expect card fee growth to accelerate in Q3 and exit Q4 in the high teens. The single biggest contributor to that inflection point is the Platinum refresh. It takes time to hit the P&L because we started repricing card members beginning in January and when we move card members to the new price point, we amortize it over 12 months. So it's a slow process and the impact is delayed. That delayed impact is why you've seen some inertia in the growth rate; it can take roughly two years to fully flow through the P&L from beginning to end. But to be clear, we expect card fees to exit this year with growth in the high teens.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Rob Wildhack of Autonomous Research.

transcript.speaker: Robert Wildhack
transcript.title: Analyst - Autonomous Research
transcript.content: A question on NII growth. First, in the quarter, growth there slowed 150 basis points from Q1 to Q2. Is there anything to call out there? And then going forward, you said to grow faster than billings, but can you unpack that a little more? You have the commercial portfolios that are drags, but on the positive side you have really strong credit outcomes which might be a reason to continue to lean into NII growth. How does that all come together in terms of growth in that line and in the context of the higher revenue guide?

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Let me clarify: there is a bit of noise in those numbers. We reported balance sheet growth of 9% which is in line with billing growth of 9%. Last quarter balance growth was 7%, so there's a step-up due to the accounting classification of two small business co-brand portfolios that were reclassified as held for sale over a year ago. We lapped that reclassification. From a P&L standpoint in the NII line, despite those portfolios being held for sale, the economics were flowing through our P&L. But in April we transferred one of those portfolios — the smaller one — to the new issuer. That transfer impacted NII growth by about 1 percentage point. So the decline you see in the NII growth rate from 12% to 11% is largely attributable to that transfer. The second transfer (of the Amazon portfolio) is expected in Q3. By Q4 both portfolios will be out of our system and the impact to NII will be roughly 2.5 percentage points until we lap it. Importantly, although it impacts NII, the impact to net income and earnings is negligible and was baked into our original guidance at the beginning of the year. So no change to guidance or earnings, but you will see discontinuity in balance growth and NII growth rates due to those portfolio transfers.

transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Darrin Peller of Wolfe Research.

transcript.speaker: Darrin Peller
transcript.title: Analyst - Wolfe Research
transcript.content: I wanted to touch on operating leverage. I know you've said you're going to be reinvesting quite a bit of the top line upside into customer acquisition. But just for a minute about deploying AI within customer service and internal functions: where are you seeing pacing on that now? When would you expect to see some incremental benefits show up in a more material way?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Darrin, thanks for the question. Let me ask Christophe to address operating leverage pacing for the rest of the year and then I'll talk about AI.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: The way we define operating leverage is OpEx as a ratio of revenue. OpEx for us is annualized between roughly $16 billion and $17 billion. There are a variety of items that hit that line, and quarter-to-quarter you can see discrete one-offs. If you take a step back over many years, we've been effective at driving operating leverage in terms of OpEx to revenue, and we are committed to continuing that. AI will play a critical role and is part of the reason we're investing. For the balance of the year, we expect operating expense growth to be in the mid-single digits for the full year, and we're tracking well against that. This quarter OpEx grew 6%, and we expect to be in the mid-single-digit range by year end. Steve can elaborate on what we're working on with AI.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: On AI: most companies are engaging with it, but not many have committed to explicit P&L savings for 2026 or 2027. We've deployed AI in multiple places. In technology, we're seeing 30% to 40% decreases in cycle time for coding. That's not pure savings because it allows us to do more — we have a large backlog of tech projects and AI helps us get to them faster. In servicing — travel and card servicing — we've equipped customer service and travel agents with AI-powered tools and seen a reduction in the need to accelerate hiring even as the business grows. Over time we expect the number of representatives to decrease or at least not scale linearly with business volume due to AI-driven productivity gains. In marketing, AI streamlines campaign development and reduces time-to-market, which converts to faster time-to-money. We've used AI in credit, risk and fraud for many years, but now we're integrating unstructured data and agentic capabilities to improve decisioning. Integration matters: embedding AI into systems or putting layers above them is required to make it seamless. For example, we launched a servicing portal for our customer service representatives with embedded AI that reduces handle time and improves customer experience. We are further along on AI than in agentic e-commerce; agentic commerce is in earlier innings. We have high hopes that AI will make us more efficient, more productive, and ultimately drive top-line and earnings growth over time.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: The next question is coming from Bill Carcache of Piper Sandler.

transcript.speaker: Bill Carcache
transcript.title: Analyst - Piper Sandler
transcript.content: Good morning, Steve and Christophe. You've both been with Amex for many years. As investors debate Amex's valuation versus history, it would be helpful to get your thoughts: as you reflect on your years with the company, what has fundamentally changed about Amex's product flywheel that makes the growth algorithm more durable today than it was historically? And what gives you confidence that the rebuilt product flywheel can compound beyond the current refresh cycle rather than just requiring repeated reinvestment to sustain growth?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Squeri
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thank you. I've been here many years and Christophe also has long tenure. When we step back, what's changed is we have committed more to truly understanding customer needs and where customers are going. This business is all about the customer, and customer needs evolve. Product refreshes are critical because needs change. Another change is we've expanded our aperture of who our customer is. We still focus on high-spending, high-creditworthy premium aspirational customers, but previously we defined that as a specific cohort. Now we recognize those customers exist across Boomers, Gen X, Millennials and Gen Z. We built a product ecosystem that can adapt to the next cohorts rather than using a one-size-fits-all product. The Platinum product, for example, can play well across generations because we can add value in ways that apply broadly. We've also leaned more into partners — co-brand and premium partners who want access to our customers and are willing to provide benefits. Limited-time offers and partner access are important. We've also changed our international approach, focusing our coverage on the U.K., Mexico, Canada, Australia and Japan — that has paid off. Putting it together across consumer, travel, restaurants and experiences, plus investments in lounges and fine hotels and resorts, we create a premium ecosystem that's durable. Partners want to play in it. The durability is reinforced by momentum and the ability to reinvest over time. We're not looking at just a year; we look at medium to long term. From $30 billion in revenue in 2017 to about $70 billion now, we have more scale and more ability to operate. That scale, combined with a product flywheel that adapts to cohorts, partnerships and international focus, makes our growth algorithm more durable and gives us confidence that reinvestment today compounds into long-term growth.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: I'll add a finance perspective. There's more momentum today than 10–15 years ago across product refresh pace and revenue momentum. The resilience of the portfolio is stronger: reserves have declined from 2.9% at the end of 2019 to 2.7% now, reflecting a premium portfolio. Card fees have grown meaningfully; that line has grown at 17% over the last seven years because more card members pay fees. Stress testing also shows we have much lower peak write-off rates than competitors and we're profitable through a severely adverse cycle. Finally, focusing on younger card members gives us confidence in sustaining growth: they may start with lower income but we grow with them, which represents embedded long-term growth.

transcript.speaker: Christophe Le Caillec

Our expectation is that the positive momentum will continue through the balance of the year, with that co-brand transfer headwind factored into our planning.
